convention: RESOLVED: iia's one-letter items `p`, `n` and `k` are the fertilizer MACRONUTRIENTS -- phosphate, nitrogen and potash -- not corrupt item labels. 890 valued rows, all in tonnes, all within 1909-1933, across ~50 countries, medians p=85,464 n=14,638 k=55,192 t. The panel SEPARATELY carries `commercial phosphoric acid`, `commercial nitrogenous fertilizers` and `commercial potash fertilizers` from fao1952 for the DISJOINT era 1949-1951 -- the same triple, explicitly named. THEY MAY NOT BE CONCATENATED INTO ONE SERIES. Whether the two are the same MEASURE is NOT established: there is zero (country, year) overlap, so the panel cannot answer it, and the cross-era continuity test refuses the licence -- normalised to tonnes, last-iia against first-fao1952 scatters from x0.01 to x6,380 (median x0.45 / x2.71 / x1.10 for p / n / k). The direction points at a basis difference rather than growth: chile nitrogen x0.02 and egypt phosphate x0.03 are both major EXPORTERS of those materials, and 440,632 t of phosphate is not Egyptian consumption in 1933, so iia's series may be production or trade of fertilizer materials where fao1952's is consumption. Treat them as two distinct series until a source page settles the basis. PARTIALLY REFUTED 2026-08-18, BY ME, AND THE REFUTATION MATTERS MORE THAN THE PART THAT STANDS. What stands: these items are about fertilizer nutrients rather than anything else a single letter might abbreviate, and they must not be concatenated with fao1952's `commercial *` series. What is WRONG is the implication that a `p` or `n` series is a NUTRIENT TOTAL. Traced cell by cell against the raw extract, these series OSCILLATE between distinct fertilizer MATERIALS year to year: sweden's `p` reads calcium superphosphate 1909-1920 (102,509 to 185,320 t), then BASIC SLAG 1930-1932 (14,520 / 10,171 / 7,730 -- a x0.08 step), then superphosphate again in 1933 (219,030, a x28 step back). japan's `n` is calcium cyanamide throughout except 1919 (ammonium sulfate, x27) and 1933 (ammonium sulfate, x5). Also affected: norway p (x17 superphosphate vs natural phosphate), austria p and n, belgium p (basic slag vs superphosphate vs natural phosphate), france p, united kingdom p, canada n, united states p and n, japan p. These are NOT interchangeable quantities -- superphosphate, basic slag, natural phosphate rock, ammonium sulfate and calcium cyanamide are different materials with different nutrient contents -- so a `p` series is a patchwork of materials, not P2O5, and its level shifts are product switches rather than changes in fertiliser use. Do not read a trend from one. The switches go BACK AND FORTH, so growth cannot explain them.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-18 against consolidated_layer_b.parquet (192,670 rows, aggregates excluded). Items `p`/`n`/`k` are the only item labels in the whole panel shorter than 3 characters (359 distinct (source, item) pairs scanned; no digits-only, vowel-less or null-ish labels exist at all), so this is not a general label-corruption problem. p: 522 rows, n: 332, k: 36. Units are exclusively `tonnes`; fao1952's commercial* siblings are in `1000 tonnes`, which is why a naive merge would also be off by 1000 before any basis question. Eras strictly disjoint (iia max 1933 < fao1952 min 1949). Cross-era ratios computed on 27 (p), 23 (n) and 5 (k) countries present in both under normalised labels -- the first attempt found ZERO shared countries because iia lowercases and fao1952 title-cases, which is itself a trap for anyone joining these two.
retest: 2026-08-18 re-measured (11_retest_conventions.py, check_iia_npk): asserts the identification (row count, tonnes-only units, 1909-1933 span, ~50 countries, nutrient-scale medians), the disjoint fao1952 commercial* era, zero country-year overlap, AND re-derives the cross-era ratio spread, requiring it to exceed 1000x so the entry cannot silently become a licence to concatenate. 2026-08-18: the identification and the no-concatenation rule re-measured and hold; the nutrient-total implication was refuted by per-cell tracing against the raw extract (see the convention text). check_iia_npk still tests only the parts that stand.

convention: RESOLVED: iia `wine` in layer B is HECTOLITRES converted at 0.097 tonnes per hectolitre, and the raw IIA extract converted the SAME hectolitres at 0.091. That ratio, 0.097/0.091 = 1.065934066, is the unexplained factor reported in issue 358 -- every layer-B wine value is exactly 1.0659x the raw extract's because the two applied different densities to one underlying figure. It is not a must-to-wine yield, a revision or an error. The originals are whole hectolitres: germany 1909 is 2,020,620 hl, which the raw extract carries as 183,876.42 t (x0.091) and layer B as 196,000.14 t (x0.097). WHICH FACTOR IS CORRECT IS A POLICY QUESTION, NOT A MEASUREMENT. Wine density is about 0.99 kg/l, so 0.099 t/hl would be physical; layer B's 0.097 is closer to that than the extract's 0.091, so layer B is arguably the better of the two rather than the wrong one. Neither is 0.099, and the choice belongs to whoever set the pipeline's conversion table. CONSEQUENCE FOR CONSUMERS: a wine tonnage traced back to an IIA yearbook page will not match, because the page prints hectolitres and the panel prints an assumed mass. Compare hectolitres, or divide the panel figure by 0.097 to recover them exactly.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-18. 350 single-value (label, year) pairs between layer B and the raw extract give a ratio whose median, p10 and p90 are all 1.065934, on 333 of 350; the 17 exceptions are years where the raw side carries more than one row. Recovering the unit: of 1,233 raw wine production values 477 are non-integer, and dividing those by 0.091 lands on integers with a median distance from an integer of 0.000000 -- a scan of 100,000 candidate divisors between 0.05 and 0.15 found 0.091 to be the ONLY one that does. On the layer-B side, 100% of values divide by 0.097 to within 0.01 of an integer (median distance 0.00000000), against 0.7% for 0.091. Note 53.3% also divide evenly by 0.100, because many hectolitre figures are multiples of 1,000; the 100% result for 0.097 is what settles it. The first scan was degenerate and had to be redone: 756 of the raw values are ALREADY integers, so dividing them by 0.1 trivially yields integers and made 0.1 look like the answer.
retest: 2026-08-18 re-measured (11_retest_conventions.py, check_iia_wine_hectolitres): asserts that every layer-B iia wine tonnage divides by 0.097 into a whole hectolitre figure, that the raw extract's non-integer values divide by 0.091, and that 0.097/0.091 reproduces the reported 1.0659 factor.

convention: RESOLVED (measurement only; the REMEDY is still open, see issue #273): the label reports METROPOLITAN JAPAN, exclusive of Korea and Formosa/Taiwan, which this source reports under their own labels straight through. convention: Mitchell's South African CATTLE series is assembled from TWO labels, and the second one's name is misleading. `cape natal` is a single-item label -- cattle in heads, 33 rows, 1918-1957, and nothing else -- and it carries the NATIONAL series, not a Cape-plus-Natal provincial one. 12 of its cells (1946-1957) coincide with Mitchell's own `south africa` cattle cells and ALL 12 are equal to the digit over 12 DISTINCT values; a province cannot equal its nation cell for cell. The other 21 cells (1918-1945) fall in years where `south africa` carries no cattle value at all, so they EXTEND the national series rather than duplicating it. NO ROW MOVES: both labels already resolve to ZAF-1910-2025, so no published number changes and this is not a reroute. The convention exists to stop a later pass 'correcting' the `cape natal` rows onto a Cape or Natal polity on the strength of the name, and to stop the 21 gap-filling rows being dropped as duplicates, which would lose 21 years of national cattle. It says nothing about Mitchell's separate `natal` label (nine items, 1852-1957), which IS a genuine provincial series and must not be folded in here.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-19 against consolidated_layer_b.parquet, found while building 25_same_polity_overlaps.py for issue 355 (it reports the pair as relation `identical`, 12 shared cells / 12 equal / 12 distinct values). Shared cells 1946-1957: 12,113,000 / 12,470,000 / 12,242,000 / 11,513,000 / 11,565,000 / 11,768,000 / 11,655,000 / 11,604,000 / 11,689,000 / 11,800,000 / 12,042,000 / 12,062,000 head, identical under both labels. Cells under `cape natal` only: 1918-1930, 1934-1939, 1943, 1945 (6,852,000 rising to 12,593,000). Mitchell's `south africa` cattle series has just 33 rows over 1852-1960 and is absent across 1918-1945. DELIBERATELY NOT ARGUED FROM MAGNITUDE: '6.85M head is too many for two provinces' is the reasoning that put three IIA routings wrong (issue 377), so the test used is exact equality against a control, with a >=6 distinct-value floor so rounding coincidence cannot produce it.

convention: IIA's `australia` / `p` series is CHRISTMAS ISLAND's mined natural phosphate, not Australian output and not agricultural nutrient use. Raw `australia` DOES carry 25 natural-phosphate production rows of its own -- so unlike the Serbia case the alternative is present, not absent -- but layer B matches the Christmas Island series in 16 of 16 dated cells and the Australian one in 0 of 16, while Australia's own output runs 20x to 1,000x smaller in the same years. Australia's own series does not appear in layer B at all (0 of its 25 raw values reproduced under the `australia` label at the same year), so the harmonisation SUBSTITUTED the dependency's series for the metropole's rather than merely mislabelling it. CONSEQUENCE FOR CONSUMERS: a per-km2 or per-capita reading of 'Australian phosphate' is reading an island 2,600 km away, and this series is an exception to the iia p/n/k nutrient convention (issue 369) -- here `p` is mined rock, not fertiliser input. convention: The iia_1938_39 volume has MESLIN and SPELT TRANSPOSED, for every label carrying both. Relevant here because layer B has no `wheat` product in the source at all -- IIA publishes spelt (323 rows) and meslin (490) and zero wheat (issue 375) -- so layer-B `wheat` is assembled from those two, and anyone reconstructing it from iia_1938_39 would take the pair the wrong way round. THE TEST IS SELF-CONTROLLED and must be: 'meslin exceeds spelt' is FALSE as a general rule, since Belgium and Switzerland genuinely grew more spelt than meslin. The question asked is whether a volume disagrees with its own label's OTHER volumes, which needs no view about any country's agriculture. EIGHT LABELS, ESTABLISHED BY TWO TESTS OF DIFFERENT STRENGTH. Six show an exact MUTUAL VALUE CROSSOVER at 1933 -- each volume's figure for one product equals the other volume's figure for the other -- belgium, bulgaria, czechoslovakia, germany, spain and yugoslavia. Two more (austria, switzerland) invert by RATIO across all years without completing the crossover, each for a documented reason: austria's iia_1938_39 meslin is 0.0, a false zero of issue 414's class, though the surviving half still matches to 0.15% (1933_34 meslin production 11,582.5 against 1938_39 spelt 11,600); switzerland's later volume both rounds and revises (31,365.4 against 28,600), missing a 1% tolerance while its ratio inverts cleanly 0.43 -> 1.70. I FIRST USED THE RATIO TEST ALONE AND IT WAS WRONG ABOUT SPAIN: spain's ratio hovers near 1 (1.00 / 0.83 / 0.95), so which side of 1 it falls on is noise, and the crossover shows it plainly -- meslin 46,980 <-> 30,000 beside spelt 29,935 <-> 47,000. A ratio test cannot see a swap between near-equal values. Both sets are pinned BY IDENTITY and kept separate, since a count would pass if a label moved between them and the two kinds of evidence are not equally strong. NO MEASURED EFFECT ON PUBLISHED FIGURES, which is why this is a convention and not a data error: of 28 layer-B `wheat` cells matched to a raw spelt/meslin row at the same label, year, variable and a non-round value, ZERO come from iia_1938_39 (8 from iia_1925_26, 19 from iia_1933_34, 1 from iia_1939_45), and layer B carries no meslin, spelt or wheat item for Bulgaria at all. SEPARATELY ESTABLISHED BY THIS WORK, and load-bearing for issue 375: layer-B `wheat` draws from BOTH raw products -- 21 of the 28 solid cells from spelt and 7 from meslin -- so there is no single conversion that recovers the original, and which product a given cell is remains a per-cell fact.

convention: The iia_1938_39 volume also has CALCIUM CYANAMIDE and CALCIUM NITRATE transposed -- a second commodity pair swapped in the same volume as meslin/spelt, found by the same mutual-crossover search. Demonstrated for czechoslovakia, italy, norway and poland. NORWAY IS THE ANCHOR AND IT IS DOCUMENTARY, NOT A MAGNITUDE ARGUMENT: Norway was the home of the Birkeland-Eyde process, so calcium NITRATE ('Norwegian saltpetre') at ~163,500 t against ~23,300 t of cyanamide is the expected order in every other volume, and iia_1938_39 prints 120,400 cyanamide against 34,650 nitrate. Its cyanamide/nitrate ratio runs 0.36 / 0.27 / 0.14 across three volumes and 3.47 in this one. NO MEASURED PROPAGATION. Layer-B `n` for these labels takes the iia_1933_34 figure at 1933 -- czech republic 18,330, italy 136,591, poland 10,118 all match that volume's cyanamide exactly -- and carries no 1934-1938 rows for them at all, so the transposed volume's years never enter the panel. Recorded because anyone reading nitrogen fertiliser out of the raw extract for 1934-1938 would take the two products the wrong way round, and because it establishes that the iia_1938_39 transposition is not confined to one commodity pair.

convention: The last two yearbook volumes report on a 100-UNIT GRID; the earlier four resolve finer. Of NON-ZERO production/area values, iia_1938_39 and iia_1939_45 put 95.0% and 95.6% on a multiple of 100 (49.6%/52.1% on a multiple of 1000) with sub-unit precision at 1.5%/1.1%; iia_1909_21 through iia_1933_34 sit at 10.9-27.3% on a 100 grid with 26.9-39.6% sub-unit. A value from 1939 onward therefore carries roughly +/-50 units, not +/-0.5, and a small producer legitimately reads as a round constant.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-19 over the 62,851 NON-ZERO production/area rows of the raw IIA extract, grouped by the `yearbook` column. Zeros are excluded from numerator AND denominator: 0 satisfies every grid, so counting it makes a volume look coarse in proportion to its zero rate. On the all-values basis iia_1938_39 reads 88.9% instead of 95.0%, and that 6.1pp gap is just its false-zero rate (issue 414) leaking into a precision statistic. Corroborated independently by state/constant_runs.csv: for 169 of 170 constant runs the finer-resolution evidence sits ENTIRELY OUTSIDE the run's own years and INSIDE it in none, and the run constants (100; 1,000; 2,000; 3,000; 5,000) are exactly what survives rounding to this grid. iia run starts cluster at the volume handovers: 41% in 1933-1935 and 32% in 1939-1941.
verified_by: issue-366 re-measurement, which WITHDREW that issue's own argument: it claimed these constants could not be a resolution limit because the series resolve finer, and the finer values turned out to be cross-era in every case
retest: 2026-08-19 measured by 11_retest_conventions.py (check_iia_volume_grid): late volumes 95.0%/95.6% of non-zero values on the 100 grid against a 40% early ceiling (early max 27.3%); counter-test holds, iia_1939_45's zero rate 0.39% is ordinary while iia_1938_39's is 6.45%, so the precision boundary (1938/39) stays distinct from issue 414's zero boundary (1933/34)

convention: Mitchell REPORTS IN THOUSANDS: 88.6% of its 40,664 non-zero panel values are exact multiples of 1,000 (92.2% of 100) and only 2 rows carry any sub-unit precision. Every Mitchell figure therefore carries roughly +/-500 in its own unit and must not be read as exact. Flat in time -- 88-94% per decade from the 1890s to the 1950s -- so this is a publisher convention, not a volume or era boundary, and one constant covers the whole source.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-19 over all 40,664 non-zero non-aggregate mitchell rows of consolidated_layer_b.parquet, across ha, heads and tonnes alike. THE DISCRIMINATING NUMBER IS THE SUB-UNIT COUNT: 2 of 40,664. A high share of round values could mean a source reports round quantities; near-total absence of fractional parts cannot arise by chance. COUNTER-TEST: the sibling source fao1952 covers the same era and commodities at 1.1% on a 1000-grid with 12.0% sub-unit precision, so the coarseness is Mitchell's and not the period's. Contrast iia, whose coarseness is a per-volume boundary (12% -> 69% -> 92% across the 1920s-40s, issue 366/445).
verified_by: issue-446 measurement of panel-side precision, which also widened that issue: the exposure is 89,938 of 189,090 non-zero panel values on a 1000-grid, not the ~9,962 iia values I first reported
retest: 2026-08-19 measured by 11_retest_conventions.py (check_mitchell_thousand_grid): 88.6% of 40,664 non-zero values on a 1000-grid, sub-unit precision on 2 rows (0.00%), sibling fao1952 1.1% -- coarseness is source-specific, not era-wide

convention: SCOPED TO THE `heads` UNIT: juan's LIVESTOCK counts are reported in thousands. 89.1% of its 13,285 non-zero `heads` values are exact multiples of 1,000 and only 2 rows carry any sub-unit precision, so every juan livestock figure carries roughly +/-500 head. THIS IS NOT A CLAIM ABOUT juan AS A WHOLE, which is a mixture: 47.2% of all its non-zero values sit on a 1000-grid with 14.8% sub-unit, and the share rises monotonically from 44% in the 1900s to 89% in the 1950s, so no single constant describes the source and none is recorded here. Its crop axis is measurably finer -- ha 49.3% on a 1000-grid with 13.0% sub-unit, tonnes 34.1% with 20.3%.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-19 over all non-zero non-aggregate juan rows of consolidated_layer_b.parquet. THE DISCRIMINATING NUMBER IS THE SUB-UNIT COUNT: 2 of 13,285. A high share of multiples of 1,000 could mean a source reports round herd sizes; near-total absence of fractional parts cannot arise that way. THE CONTROL IS INTERNAL, which is stronger than the cross-source control the mitchell entry uses: juan's own ha and tonnes rows are measured in the same run and are not coarse, so the coarseness cannot be an artefact of the pipeline or of the era. WITHDRAWN GENERALISATION: I first read this as livestock being thousand-reported by every publisher, citing mitchell/heads at 100.0%. That is circular -- mitchell rounds everything, its tonnes are 78.2% on a 1000-grid with 0.01% sub-unit -- and only juan and mitchell carry `heads` at all, so there is no third publisher to separate 'livestock is rounded' from 'these two compilers round' (issue 446).
verified_by: issue-446 panel-side precision measurement; the within-juan unit contrast is what survived after the cross-source livestock generalisation was tested and withdrawn
retest: 2026-08-19 measured by 11_retest_conventions.py (check_juan_heads_thousand_grid): 89.1% of 13,285 non-zero `heads` values on the 1000 grid, sub-unit precision on 2 rows; internal control juan ha/tonnes far finer, so the coarseness is the livestock axis rather than the source

convention: The item is a GROUP, not a commodity: fao1952 holds ONE ROW PER MEMBER under it, and the member is identified only by ROW ORDER, which is ALPHABETICAL -- pos0=asses, pos1=horses, pos2=mules. NOT the order the item name lists them in (horses, mules, asses); recovering these by trusting the item name's sequence mislabels every row. 945 rows, 160 complete triples. The same shape (one source sheet, one indicator, a consistent small row count per country-year) holds for fao1952 `meat` (145 groups of 4), `poultry` (106 of 4) and `other meat`, but their members exist nowhere else in the panel so their order is NOT established and must not be assumed alphabetical by analogy.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-21. `juan` and `mitchell` carry `asses`, `horses` and `mules and hinnies` as SEPARATE items, giving an independent reference. For every fao1952 3-row group where all three members are independently available, all six position-to-member permutations were scored (match within 2%): 71 groups testable, 51 with a unique best permutation, 45 matching all three positions, and the winning permutation was pos0=asses/pos1=horses/pos2=mules in 51 of 51 -- no other permutation won in a single group. Exact cases: Algeria 1950 fao [325, 217, 238] vs ref asses 325 / horses 217 / mules 238; Algeria 1951 [338, 215, 234] vs 338 / 215 / 234; Albania 1938 [45, 54, 10] vs 44 / 54 / 10. UNITS MUST BE ALIGNED FIRST: the reference is in `heads` and fao1952 in `1000 heads`, and without that the unit mismatch dominates the distance so every position matches whichever member is smallest -- a uniform answer that is the tell. CONSEQUENCE: a consumer keyed on (item, unit, year) sees three values under one item; the mean collapse measured on issue 367 returns 566.7 for Afghanistan 1949 (rows 1000/500/200), which is neither the 1,700 total nor any of the three animals.
retest: 2026-08-20 re-measured (11_retest_conventions.py): 71 testable 3-row groups, 51 with a unique best permutation, 45 exact, and pos0=asses/pos1=horses/pos2=mules winning 51 of 51 with no other permutation ever winning.
